content:
Have you ever turned on the radio and felt like every pop song sounds the same? Or watched a horror movie and predicted the ending after 20 minutes?

In a new paper published in *Frontiers in Psychology*, researchers from the Singapore Management University and James Cook University Singapore argue that "hyper-selection" arises in highly competitive environments—where people become increasingly adept at identifying and optimising what works, and keep selecting for the same traits rather than experimenting with alternatives.

The result is a blow to creativity. In an increasingly optimisation-driven world, "hyper-selection" could make everything from music to urban planning to football matches more mundane.

Research psychologist and lead author Jose C. Yong likens "hyper-selection" to natural selection—the evolutionary process by which individuals with advantageous traits or more effective strategies are more likely to survive and reproduce. Modern technology has made this selection process unusually rapid and intense.

Yong says: "We can now identify what works best, replicate it almost immediately, and keep optimising it. When there are strong selection pressures—such as intense competition or severe consequences for not optimising—this process accelerates."

Optimisation is generally useful, because it helps us achieve our goals more effectively. But when everyone is optimising for the same thing, other traits, behaviours, products and strategies may disappear, resulting in efficiency being gained "at the cost of the adaptability and usefulness that come with diversity or variation."

When we fall into "hyper-selection," we miss out on creative masterpieces like "Bohemian Rhapsody."

When explaining the concept to people unfamiliar with "hyper-selection," Yong likes to use Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" as an example. Critics in 1975 initially dismissed the song as a "bold pastiche," a "stylistic collage" that didn't fit—yet the single is now regarded as one of the greatest works in rock history, largely because the band was willing to take creative risks at the time.

"Bohemian Rhapsody" is the opposite of "hyper-selection."

Yong says: "The song is nearly six minutes long, contains wildly different musical sections, has no traditional chorus, and even includes an operatic passage—all of which make it stand apart."

Another song that clearly does not belong to "hyper-selection" is Stevie Nicks's "Edge of Seventeen," which breaks with conventional song structure and possesses an instantly recognisable sound. Yong also mentions System of a Down, noting that their songs sound "outrageously bizarre" yet still topped the charts, "precisely because their work is fresh and distinctive."

Compared with the past, today's radio hits may be more derivative and monotonous—so much so that Yong struggles to single out a representative example.

Yong says: "Honestly, I'm not sure I can point to a contemporary pop song that exemplifies 'hyper-selection.' Part of the reason is that contemporary pop songs all sound so similar that there's little that leaves a strong impression."

But he says certain music genres are a perfect embodiment of "hyper-selection"—for instance, the gloomy, breathy pop sung in hushed tones, or the "mumble-rap" that was ubiquitous a few years ago.

"Hyper-selection" is also why Yong's co-author and fellow research psychologist Edison Tan rarely listens to the radio, preferring to discover emerging, less-played indie musicians.

Tan told *HuffPost*: "It's not that my taste has changed—the world has. What I long for is rich, nuanced emotional expression, and pop music no longer offers that."

Yong says that, driven by factors such as streaming numbers, marketing reach and limited attention on social media, the music industry has already shown a clear trend toward songs that are shorter and simpler.

Beyond music, where else does "hyper-selection" appear?

Yong, Tan and their co-author Simon S. Groome say that "hyper-selection" and the pursuit of optimisation and efficiency have made nearly every aspect of life more predictable, more tedious and more uniform—and they see this pattern in sport as well.

In professional football, teams are constantly searching for tactics that can give them an edge. Once a strategy proves successful, opponents quickly follow suit. Matches become more intense and tactically more sophisticated, but teams' styles of play are also becoming increasingly similar, leaving less room for individual flair.

The same is happening in working life. Drawing on his own background, Tan uses academia as an example.

He says: "When we were doing our postgraduate studies, we were taught to be bold thinkers, to explore new ideas, to figure out how the world works."

In an ideal world, the best researchers should be the most creative problem-solvers—people who dare to think differently. But reality is far from these ideals.

Tan says: "Scholars are forced to justify their worth not by the quality of their ideas, but by metrics such as the number of papers they publish, how often they are cited, and the amount of research funding they bring in."

He adds: "The 'P' for 'Philosophy' in a PhD has long ceased to exist. When we begin to see the same pattern in other areas of life, we can't help asking whether there is some fundamental force driving these trends."

Artificial intelligence will accelerate "hyper-selection."

Yong says it almost goes without saying that AI will speed up "hyper-selection." AI is, by design, an exercise in relentless recursive optimisation, requiring little to no human intervention, and operating at speeds and scales far beyond what humans or earlier technologies could achieve.

He says: "We're already seeing this with online content—AI-generated articles, marketing copy, social media posts, images, videos, web design, and even music all sound or look remarkably similar, because they are generated from the same underlying patterns and constantly optimised based on what 'works.'"

If people consume this content unthinkingly, there will be almost no check on AI-driven "hyper-selection."

"Hyper-selection" is not entirely bad, but creators need to be aware of it.

Yong stresses that optimisation itself is not bad; it can help people achieve their goals and improve their lives. But because the pressure to optimise can be so powerful, creators may unconsciously sacrifice adaptive variation.

He says: "This is precisely the juncture at which becoming aware of 'hyper-selection' becomes crucial—and one of the reasons I want to articulate this concept clearly—is that only by recognising it can we think about what to do when it occurs."

Yong says the key is to recognise how easily we fall into the "hyper-selection" trap, and to find ways to nurture creativity and preserve diversity.

He says: "Creativity often comes from exposure to different things and recombining them in new ways. If everything looks, sounds and works the same, we lose both a reservoir of alternative strategies and the raw material from which new ideas can spring."

We also need to be more mindful of what we consume.

Yong says: "If audiences can recognise that music, films or other cultural products have become overly formulaic, and demand something more interesting, that in itself changes the selection pressures that shape production."
